title: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body
intro: What you eat every day decides how you grow, how much energy you have, and how strong your body becomes. This chapter explains why a balanced diet matters and how to build healthy eating habits.

sections.heading: Why We Eat Different Kinds of Food
bullets: Food gives us energy to move and play, materials to grow, and protection from illness.
No single food has everything our body needs, so we eat many kinds.
Different family meals around India use local, seasonal ingredients — rice in the south, wheat in the north, fish near the coast.
What you eat is shaped by where you live, the season, and family traditions.

sections.heading: Components of Food
bullets: Carbohydrates give us energy quickly — found in rice, wheat, potato, sugar.
Proteins help us grow and repair body parts — found in dal, paneer, eggs, fish, milk.
Fats give us energy that lasts longer and store warmth — found in butter, ghee, oils, nuts.
Vitamins and minerals keep us healthy and prevent diseases — found in fruits, vegetables, milk.
Dietary fibre (roughage) helps the body get rid of waste — found in whole grains, fruits, vegetables.
Water is needed for almost every process in the body.

sections.heading: Plant and Animal Sources
bullets: Plant sources include grains (rice, wheat), pulses (dal), vegetables, fruits, oils, and spices.
Animal sources include milk, curd, eggs, fish, meat.
Some foods come from many parts of a plant — leaves (spinach), roots (carrot), stem (sugarcane), seeds (rice), and fruits (mango).
Honey comes from bees, but the nectar bees collect comes from plants.

sections.heading: Testing Foods for Their Components
bullets: Iodine solution turns blue-black on a food that contains starch — rice, potato test positive.
When you rub a food on plain paper and let it dry, an oily mark means the food contains fat — peanut, butter test positive.
Boiling food with copper sulphate and caustic soda turns violet if protein is present — egg, dal test positive.
These simple tests show how scientists check what is inside a food.

sections.heading: Building a Balanced Diet
bullets: A balanced diet has the right amount of every food component, not just one or two.
Eating only sweets or only fried food gives energy but no proteins, vitamins, or fibre.
A simple thali pattern — roti, dal, rice, vegetable, curd, salad — gives most components together.
Fruit at any meal helps add vitamins and fibre.
Drinking enough clean water through the day is part of the balance.

sections.heading: Healthy Eating Habits
bullets: Wash hands before eating and after using the washroom.
Wash fruits and vegetables before cutting or eating them.
Eat freshly cooked food when possible; covered, refrigerated food stays safe longer.
Eat slowly, chew well, and stop when you feel full — this is mindful eating.
Don't waste food; take only what you can finish.

sections.heading: When the Diet Goes Wrong
bullets: A diet missing one or more nutrients leads to deficiency diseases.
Too little protein in young children causes weakness and stunted growth.
Too little iron leads to anaemia (tiredness, pale skin).
Too little vitamin A can affect eyesight; too little vitamin D can weaken bones.
These diseases can usually be prevented or cured by adding the missing food group back.

key_takeaways: Food gives energy, helps growth, and protects against illness.
Carbohydrates and fats give energy; proteins help growth; vitamins and minerals protect us.
Fibre and water are essential even though they don't give energy by themselves.
A balanced diet has every food component in the right amount.
Simple tests like iodine for starch and paper for fat reveal what a food contains.
Clean hands, fresh food, and not wasting food are part of mindful eating.

glossary.definition: A substance in food the body uses to live, grow, and stay healthy.
A nutrient that gives quick energy, found in rice, wheat, sugar.
A nutrient that builds and repairs the body, found in dal, milk, eggs.
A nutrient that gives long-lasting energy, found in oils, butter, nuts.
A nutrient needed in small amounts to keep the body healthy and prevent disease.
A nutrient like iron or calcium needed in small amounts for bones, blood, and teeth.
Plant material the body cannot digest but helps clear waste.
Food that has the right amount of every nutrient the body needs.
An illness caused by missing one or more nutrients in the diet.
Eating slowly, paying attention to food, and stopping when full.
